text: Beijing is an ancient capital in northern China. Its long history goes back more than three thousand years. Today about twenty-one million people live in the city region. Guidebooks say that the pace of life in Beijing is very fast: people hurry between skyscrapers, ring roads fill with cars at rush hour, and meetings often start on time. Citizens are proud of their culture—the Temple of Heaven, the Forbidden City, and of course famous Beijing roast duck on a family dinner table. When we compare two cities, we use comparative adjectives such as faster, busier, or older to describe polite differences.

Chengdu is a lively city in southwest China. It also has a recorded history of more than three thousand years. Like Beijing, the population is about twenty-one million. However, many travel writers say that daily life in Chengdu feels slower and more relaxing: teahouses stay noisy until late at night, parks fill with chess players, and friends enjoy long spicy hotpot dinners. Chengdu is famous for giant pandas that attract families from around the world. Students sometimes joke that Chengdu hotpot tastes spicier than Beijing duck—let us check that idea with careful English.
Like Beijing, the population in Chengdu is about twenty-one million.
Both Beijing and Chengdu have a recorded history of more than three thousand years.
The pace of life in Beijing is faster than that in Chengdu.
Daily life in Chengdu feels more relaxing than daily life in Beijing.
Chengdu hotpot tastes spicier than Beijing duck.
Which city is more relaxing, Beijing or Chengdu?
Chengdu is more relaxing than Beijing.
Which city is busier, Beijing or Chengdu?
Fill the two blanks. Use much or a lot with spicier. Never use very before a comparative.
The hotpot in Chengdu is much spicier than the food in Beijing.
